Downvote me all you want, pessimism is never popular but its often right.

It's a zero-sum game. Everyone, and I mean everyone, is pursuing power. Power means different things, in different contexts, but it always gets back to power.

The question really is in how you do it, and who suffers as a result, and how far you take it. It's very easy to swing the pendulum back too far, and end up in a society that may or may not be any better but just different.

No longer content to use the network as the boundary, they also want a boundary inside the computer. comment_text.value:
> People know how the sites they visit are funded and need some way to justify cutting that off.

As the admin for various SMBs I cared only in a vague, way whether their browsing experience was made unpleasant by ads.

I cared enormously whether I had to spend valuable time imaging or de-rooting their PC because some 0-click infection delivered by ad-network ransomwared us.

I have never felt even the slightest obligation to the vague collective of websites that rely on the shockingly dangerous concept of injecting unvetted, advertiser-supplied code into trusted domains.

From the moral angle, paywalls are an option and were in fact heavily used 25 years ago. The decision to rely for revenue on whether and in what manner a browser renders certain elements is certainly a choice a site-operator can make but it creates neither legal nor moral obligations on me or my users. My obligations as a paid IT / security practitioner are rather clear, and they are to my employers and clients.

I do not know the latest numbers on "what percent of web-based (or all) infections are mitigated by adblocking", but based on historicals that it is well over 50%. In that context it is lunacy to ask "but what about the site operators who create this mess".

story_title.value: I wish tech companies knew more about me

comment_text.value:
I enjoyed reading your commentary but didn't find that it supports your musing here: "I think about the Fermi Paradox. What if the answer to why there are no galactic civilizations is as simple as "because capitalism"? "

That wouldn't make any sense, because if it were true then we wouldn't have seen the population explosion take off under a primarily dominant global capitalist economy in the first place. The ability to distribute goods and services in a decentralized way and accompanying technological advances which are supported by market opportunities focused on profit have paved the way for the 8+ billion people on the planet who are almost all living in much better conditions than most human beings throughout history. I'd argue if anything capitalism enabled overpopulation, not the inverse.

With respect to birth rates I believe there are a lot of factors at play, but one which is perhaps the largest is the substitution of the family unit with the state. Even as little as 100 years ago we were a lot more family-oriented with much of that seeming to dissolve recently. We don't need a child or 5 to take care of us when we're older, we have a 401k and an HSA for that. There are pros and cons there.

The mix of factors influencing declining birthrates I would argue depend on the country. South Korea is a homogenous country of 50+ million about the size of Indiana. There are too many people for too few opportunities and everyone wants the good life. That's why people are spending their life savings on tutors for their children, unlike the United States perhaps where while we have quite a number of people living we are the world's most diverse country and here we have (for now) enough opportunity for folks to pursue careers, start new businesses, and such.

story_title.value: Children of Men: The future is a mirror for the present

comment_text.value:
I would suggest reading some history rather than economic fantasy.

It's not "a competitive environment" just because it's legal to found a company if anticompetitive tactics are allowed.

You can start a railroad, but if the big existing railroads that already have lines running to the cities and factories refuse to let you connect to their service, your company has no hope of surviving.

You can start a factory making paperclips, but if the incumbent has billions of dollars in reserves and can afford to sell at a loss or barely above cost you will never be able to grow and thrive.

You can make a lot more money talking to your competitors and agreeing to fix prices or to each operate in regions that happen to not overlap, eliminating competition.

You can tell customers that if they want to buy product X that they want, they have to buy a bundle that includes Y, meaning that any competitors to Y are bound to fail since customers are already buying that version anyway.

This is just the tip of the iceberg. "History of antitrust" will give you any number of real world examples.

comment_text.value:
The coolest thing about studying very ancient history is the realization that you are starting both at a new beginning and also deeply in medias res.

You are right there at the beginning of cities and written language and entities recognizable as "governments" and record-keeping and all sorts of other things.

And yet you are millennia removed from the first large-scale organized societies, towns, building projects, non-nomadic agricultural practices, arts such as painting pottery, poetry/storytelling, language itself, and societal tropes and stereotypes and concepts -- concepts such as "greed" or "happiness", as well as social structures such as rulers and slaves and merchants and everyone in between.

What a strange time it must have been: writing was new technology at the time, and yet people were very much the same as they had already been for thousands of years prior, and of course are much the same as they are today. Add to it the substantial climactic and geographical changes that have occurred in the millennia since then, and the combined result is both uncannily familiar and extremely alien.

It's also fascinating to consider what changed and didn't change in the intervening thousands of years, and at different rates and in different directions in various parts of the world. Ancient Sumer would have been just as alien to a citizen of Roman or Sassanian Mesopotamia as the Meosopotamia of classical antiquity would be to someone living there today.

WHAT?!?

This is a wild statement to make.

The pace of AI development and adoption has been insanely fast compared to virtually every major technological revolution in history.

* Chat GPT: ~3 years from GPT-2 "it kinda chats with you" to GPT-6 Astra "It's writing entire code bases"

In college, we had a CDC Cyber running NOS.

For programming, they taught us enough to use the XEDIT line editor, the Fortran compiler, CATLIST for the directory.

You'd apply these in rote fashion, the goal was to get through your programming class. It wasn't an a OS design or computer architecture class. It was "calculate Easter Sunday in Fortan" class.

Our Fortran (F77) used channels 4 and 5 for console in and out (which could probably be redirected using some command, no doubt. I don't know if it was. NOS thing or some Fortran thing that we used 4 and 5.

But it had these other things that you'd touch on, if you were geeking a bit in the community. Things like Direct Storage using the ATTACH command (whatever that did), PROC files (scripts), PROC file libraries, DAYFILE (basically your job/command history).

I would like to have a deeper understanding about some of those concepts of how that OS worked, design choices they needed to make, etc.

Today, "everything" is UNIX. Or certainly viewed through UNIX glasses. Even Windows is UNIX today.

I don't know how it might sound like but trust me when I say this, but as someone from third world country, 10$ can still buy us a lot and is a force to be reckoned with.

Especially as a teen as I am and the frugality that I usually hold close to my heart, just as a reference, my monthly budget of me and my friends within college is usually around 30-40$ and I think that I live very comfortably for what its worth.

Alas, I don't think that I would be here if the permanent account costed me 10$, I am sure that I might have read an occasional or two or lurked out here for sometime but I would've lost my interest if it not were for my ability to comment or make account easily/for free within my particular use case. So for me, its hard to support this model given that it would've excluded people like me in the first place (whom I am not sure how many are there though but I certainly talk a lot about Hackernews to my friends) but I still understand from where the rationale is coming from.

I do not know what the ideal form of community formation on the internet is, perhaps its a form of tradeoffs and there would be some community which might still be disenfranchised in this battle against bots.

From my personal opinion, there should be a way to show that some human effort has been placed within the community. Yet its a chicken and egg problem as giving the opportunity to showcase that can also invariably lead to them breaking that trust and spamming (and doing bot-like activities).

Maybe some form of system where people can write words say for example on blog and then they can get a score in terms of how much human effort is put into it. Maybe if we can show that some person wrote for 10 minutes on a keyboard or an hour showcasing the rough drafts from start to finish, it can be worthy exercise and then we can sort of have some key which can be verified with that level of human effort which we can then use to sign up to multiple forums.

I don't think that this last idea is the end-all be-all and I might even cringe reading it in a few years if my account is still up perhaps, but I think that there's really lots of potential in who can discover an good enough way of detecting human effort put in/for a community without having bots infesting the place.

Perhaps Monetary form is just one way of showing that as money is still one of the very few things left which we get in transaction of human effort and it is one thing that shows human effort without being infested with bots except the fact that an unequal amount of money is given for unequal amount of human effort. Some get less and some more which as in the case was mine could disenfranchise people.

It's gonna be interesting nonetheless though to see what tradeoffs are adopted by internet in this war against bots. I wonder what historians will think of this as people trying to re-invent town halls as the previous town-halls of the internet got infested with rats because it got too big to clean and the algorithmic incentives of profits rather than the cleanliness of it all.

This depends heavily on what time frame you're talking about.

For much of history people would often have children to work on farms and support the parents when they're older. Sometimes this support system was nuclear. Sometimes it was broader in society. So how do you account for "expensive" here? I honestly don't know.

But a lot of people focus on more modern times, particularly post-WW2, because the trend here is pretty much straight up. Education, housing and medical expenses have far exceeded inflation and real wages.

In more developed Asian countries (eg South Korea, Japan, China) the number of children has gone down in part because it is so expensive. In South Korea, so much is spent on tutoring to get into a good university to get a good job. The entire family's income is devoted to that. In China, for a man to be marriageable he often needs to pay the bride's family, have property, have a good job and so on. China has actually tried tackling some of this by popping the real estate bubble and outlawing private tutoring. Still, competition is intense and the bride price is still very real.

I think about the Fermi Paradox. What if the answer to why there are no galactic civilizations is as simple as "because capitalism"? Birth rates in developed countries are generally falling off a cliff as the barrier-to-entry gets increasingly higher.

What?

NXP's i.MX 7 was released in 2013 with Cortex-A7 + Cortex-M4 and well supported back then. And there probably were earlier chips.

Yeah Linux is slow at developing features for embedded systems. That's why embedded programmers run code outside of Linux. Fortunately, Linux has kernel modules to make it easy to do things like that.

Historically, Linux isn't even a proper embedded OS. Linux continues to get better-and-better for embedded but I'd expect that 2013-era was dominated by VxWorks or other embedded OSes with a better featureset for embedded. It was _LINUX_ that was the problem in my experience, at least back then.

But then WindRiver (makers of VxWorks) added a bunch of features to the Linux kernel and now today Linux is acceptable for embedded. I dunno exactly when the switchover from majority VxWorks embedded systems -> WindRiver Linux -> and now each manufacturer has their own BSP / Linux support... but a lot of what you're complaining about was software development.

Even then, a ton of older embedded crap ran their own custom versions of Linux 2.4 or whatever and just maintained a separate branch. I'm guessing these older embedded systems got their start in the early 00s and just had issues upgrading past the Linux 2.4 -> Linux 2.6 jump.

Or in other words: it was far more likely that Linux wouldn't support Chip X, rather than Chip X was unable to support Linux. Or maybe a chip did support Linux but most of the codebase was stuck on Linux 2.4. Or if Linux support existed, it was effectively proprietary custom kernel modules that individual teams wrote for themselves rather than a community-driven internet-based workflow. Etc. etc. Linux was harder back then.

But the stuff you're talking about is early 2010s, if not 00s. Damn well over a decade, might be closer to TWO decades (and the only reason I don't know that is because I was a wee-little ignorant student back then and don't really know things older than 2010s....)

I'm pretty negative on Wikipedia so my reflex was, "good." Wikipedia taught me that history is written by the victors, and today, the victors are the owners of social and news media, and the editors and moderators of Wikipedia. I used to be heavily involved in a page I won't mention, and it was well cited and factually correct. For political reasons, moderators with higher standing than me gradually removed sections, edited them unfairly, and generally vandalised the page. All sanctioned by the Wikipedia process. I learned that my page was FAR from the only page where useful, factual information was removed and edited in dishonest ways for ideological reasons. I have no doubt it's happening all over the site for many reasons. Most people don't see the politics which goes on behind the scenes, and they don't understand how much this undermines the trust in the information. My trust in the site could not be any lower than it is. I trust the parametric knowledge inside LLMs more now.

Honestly, I think knowledge like this is going to organically synchronise with consensus nodes in the very near future. Think of Community Notes on X as a prototype. That doesn't mean everything will be 100% accurate at all times, but I have zero doubt that it will be infinitely better than Wikipedia.

If that is all you have then the next chess move will be random (or whatever token is more likely in isolation), or the stock prediction will be the same.

For the chess example to work you need the current board state in the context or the move history. How an LLM performs will depend on what it has learned across the transformer layers and in the residual stream, as well as how much chess data it has been trained on. -- NN models like Leela and Stockfish have been trained on thousands/millions of games and have a game-specific state space representation.

The stock prediction example is similar, but doesn't have a consistent state space in which to make that prediction. It will need information in its context (current news articles, stock history of all stocks, etc.) in order to be able to make a prediction. Its performance will depend on whether it has been able to learn factors that make it possible to make accurate predictions.

comment_text.value:
Oh, C++.

C++ feels like an old lover who I think fondly of. We were together many years, until about C++20, through thick and thin. It was exhilarating - blazingly fast, perhaps irresponsibly so, but heck, the ride was wild. It taught me so many things, and shaped me into the programmer I am today. But we went our separate ways when its shortcomings became too large to bear, and its behavior - too often undefined - no longer excusable.

I keep up with it because I still have love for it, but I have to admit I am deeply concerned about many of the life choices it is making. I should have seen how problematic it was, because I knew its history, but I had hope that it could change, and it just looks like it never will.

I'm still rooting for C++, even though I am very happy with my new primary language, Rust. I hope it changes to the better, because I really want the best for it, but right now I'm just not seeing it. It keeps repeating old mistakes (e.g., more UB footguns with every new feature), without addressing any of the big flaws (insufficient tools for building robust software).

I sometimes still write C++, but I'm not excited about it the way I used to be. When I do write C++, it's because I have to. When given the choice, Rust is simply just a better choice for almost everything I do. Right now, I don't see a future for C++ and me.

story_title.value: Ask HN: Do you still enjoy coding in C++?

I'm building Papillon: https://papillon.so, a real-time collaborative workspace for product teams.

The idea is to bring chat, docs, files, links, tasks, whiteboards and calls into one place, organised around project channels, rather than jumping between Slack, Notion, Linear, etc. I want to build a better Slack, something that feels instant, got a hacker/IDE feel to it, and works offline.

Admitting that I was taking a jab, my background (on the topic) is history and oceanography. 15 to 20 miles is (generally) well in the sub-littoral zone. Off Newport Beach - it's no flat & shallow continental shelf, but neither is it 4,000m deep ocean. In decent conditions, the shore would be obvious from atop a mast. Tall buildings might be visible to a swimmer.

"Middle of the ocean" isn't a geometric center point - but you can't make that boast if an ancient Greek fisherman would have had no problem (winds & currents willing) discerning and getting to the shore. (Note that the Mediterranean is a mere sea:)

Respecting the water, and its dangers, is a different kettle of fish. Where I live, we routinely see news about people dying in only-a-Lake Michigan. Usually within a few hundred yards of the shore, because they failed to respect the waves and currents. Every year or few, somebody drowns in the little river through town (you could throw a rock across in most spots, or wade across in quite a few). Kids (generally drunk) occasionally drown in the cute little ponds that developers dig for their new McMansion neighborhoods. Public swimming pools have lifeguards for good reason. Toddlers can drown in a 5 gallon bucket.

I am also a European. Our oligarchy looks different for sure (and look into the history of pedophile scandals in Belgium, BTW).

I am not as optimistic as you. We seem to be stagnating our way into a stark choice between becoming an American tech vassal, a Chinese tech vassal, or losing out the remnants of our ability to compete on the world markets. Half of the continent borrows money at an unsustainable rate in order to pay millions of people to do nothing for decades.

We have made decisions that looked reasonable at the time they were made, but too much has changed in the meantime and now we are stuck in bad equilibria.

The Bismarckian pay-as-you-go pension system was stable as long as people had plenty of kids and died, on average, a few years after retiring. Now they have one kid and spend 20 years in retirement before they die. The maths of that system just does not work out anymore.

The European highly regulated industry was king as long as the rest of the world had no other choice, but now that Asia has industrialized, they are blowing us out of the water. First with lower prices, but now also with quality. German exports are half of what they used to be, with another halving expected. And of course without exports, our current social spending cannot be sustained either - you cannot keep such a massive redistribution mechanism running on an economy based on selling each other cups of coffee in a beach bar.

Our most talented engineers tend to move abroad and stay there. Brain drain is one of the most serious things that can happen to a country or a continent, and we are suffering from it.

We just cannot continue to live like that, something will have to yield, but many voters just don't want to hear that.

comment_text.value:
Now imagine somebody could just describe some damage to their drywall in a text message to their computer, and it'd be magically patched away. Suffice to say, nobody would be calling in for drywall repair.

Before computers, there were computers. [1] It's obvious in hindsight, but all of these complex numerical calculations we take for granted were often not done by the same people applying them in various ways. They'd hire computers instead, which were human calculators whose job it was to do the math.

The reason these jobs no longer exist is because calculators/computers not only solved these tasks, but completely trivialized the process to do so. We're entering into a world where many cognitive tasks, including software development, are going to be trivialized in a similar fashion - describe the problem, get an answer.

And I think this is going to do similar things to what calculators and computers did (or widespread literacy for a more historical example). The ability to e.g. write a program will no longer be a valuable skill in and of itself, but simply an expectation of anybody in any role where it might be desirable to do so.

[1] - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_(occupation)

story_title.value: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
